Large, randomized, DBPCTs in children aged 5–17 years with tree pollen allergy and those aged 5–11 years with HDM-induced disease showed consistent reductions of approximately 20–22% in combined symptom and medication scores versus placebo, alongside significant improvements in disease-specific QoL despite free access to rescue medication. Treatment effects were evident across subgroups, including in children with and without asthma, and were supported by immunological markers of tolerance (increased allergen-specific IgG4 levels and blocking activity) [ , ]. Compared to pharmacotherapy, SLIT tablets generally match or exceed symptom relief, with some studies showing greater relative effects than montelukast or oral antihistamines and comparable efficacy to intranasal corticosteroids for seasonal AR/C [ ]. For patients with AR/C and allergic asthma, seasonal allergen SLIT trials typically include asthma outcomes as secondary endpoints; however, HDM SLIT tablets have demonstrated significant benefits in RCTs. A pivotal trial by Virchow et al. showed an asthma exacerbation risk reduction of ≥30% with HDM SLIT-tablet and a significant 36% relative risk reduction in moderate-severe asthma exacerbations [ ]. A study by Mosbech et al. found significant reductions in ICS use with HDM SLIT tablets while maintaining asthma control, demonstrating a significant difference compared to placebo ( p = 0.004) [ ]. These findings led to the inclusion of HDM AIT in the GINA report on asthma treatment [ ]. The RWE for SLIT complements these RCT findings by demonstrating its effectiveness under routine healthcare conditions. As highlighted for SCIT, the REACT study confirmed the long-term and sustained effectiveness of AIT, including SLIT, over 9 years of follow-up [ ]. Subgroup analyses of the REACT study found that SCIT and SLIT tablets showed similarly greater reductions in AR/C prescriptions than the controls. Specifically, the SQ grass SLIT tablet demonstrated sustained reductions in AR prescriptions for up to 7 years [ ]. These findings suggest that SLIT can prevent AR progression and impede the development of asthma ( ). Moreover, early initiation of SLIT tablets in childhood provides important long-term clinical and economic benefits compared to later treatment. Evidence from the Benefits of Early Allergen Immunotherapy Initiation (BEAT) model and the Grazax Asthma Prevention (GAP) trial showed that starting SLIT at a younger age significantly reduced the risk of progression from AR to asthma [ , ]. Initiating treatment at 5 years of age decreased the risk of developing asthma by approximately 34% compared with starting treatment at 12 years. Long-term projections indicated that approximately 19% of children treated at 5 years developed asthma over 20 years, compared with 24% in whom treatment began at 7 years and 29% in whom treatment began at 12 years. In addition, SLIT demonstrated a disease-modifying effect, with sustained reductions in AR/C symptoms of approximately 22–30% during treatment and follow-up. From a health-economic perspective, earlier SLIT initiation is associated with lower long-term healthcare costs, owing to reduced asthma incidence and better disease control. Over a 20-year period, starting treatment at the age of 5 years resulted in lower cumulative costs compared to initiation at older ages. For SLIT drops, while regulatory approval is limited in the U.S. and Canada owing to high heterogeneity in studies, a product-line meta-analysis focused on the Index of Reactivity (IR) of SLIT liquid formulations for AR/C demonstrated significant efficacy. This meta-analysis, based on 25 RCTs, found that IR-SLIT liquid was significantly more effective than placebo at reducing both symptoms and medication scores ( p < 0.0001) [ ]. The RWE from the EfficAPSI study also supports the effect of liquid SLIT on the onset and progression of asthma [ ]. 3. Allergen Immunotherapy Safety AIT is widely considered safe and well-tolerated, especially when delivered under appropriate medical supervision. Although both SCIT and SLIT are effective disease-modifying interventions, their safety profiles differ in terms of the incidence, type, and severity of adverse reactions (ARs). Understanding these differences is critical for optimizing patient selection, monitoring, and counseling. 3.1. Subcutaneous Immunotherapy Safety SCIT is associated with a higher risk of systemic allergic reactions (SARs), including anaphylaxis, than SLIT; therefore, it must be administered under strict medical supervision in settings equipped for the prompt management of anaphylaxis [ , , ]. Patients are typically monitored for at least 30 min following each injection [ , ]. In conventional SCIT regimens, the occurrence of SARs, the most clinically significant ARs of AIT, is approximately 0.2% (range 0.01–0.3%) [ , ]. Surveillance studies have reported that SARs graded 3–4 according to the World Allergy Organization criteria ( ) occur in approximately 2% of patients, with two-thirds of these events observed in individuals with pre-existing asthma [ , , ]. For safety reasons, patients with severe and uncontrolled asthma (FEV 1 or peak

equipped for the prompt management of anaphylaxis [ , , ]. Patients are typically monitored for at least 30 min following each injection [ , ]. In conventional SCIT regimens, the occurrence of SARs, the most clinically significant ARs of AIT, is approximately 0.2% (range 0.01–0.3%) [ , ]. Surveillance studies have reported that SARs graded 3–4 according to the World Allergy Organization criteria ( ) occur in approximately 2% of patients, with two-thirds of these events observed in individuals with pre-existing asthma [ , , ]. For safety reasons, patients with severe and uncontrolled asthma (FEV 1 or peak flow <70% of predicted) are generally excluded from SCIT clinical trials [ , ]. Fatal events remain exceedingly rare; U.S. surveillance data from 2008 to 2016 documented approximately 1 fatality per 9 million injections, although near-fatal reactions have been reported at a rate of 5.4 per million injections [ , , ]. Uncontrolled asthma has consistently been identified as the strongest predictor of severe and near-fatal reactions [ , , , ]. The most common ARs during SCIT are local reactions (LRs) at the injection site, including itching, swelling, and redness, which typically occur within 30 min [ , , ]. Their frequencies may be underestimated because many events occur outside the physician’s office [ ]. The composition of SCIT products also influences the risk, with clinical trials indicating that allergoid-based formulations are associated with fewer ARs than natural extracts [ , , ]. The RWE supports these findings. The prospective multicenter Allergen Immunotherapy Adverse Events Registry (ADER), which included 755 SCIT courses in adults, confirmed that both the subcutaneous route and presence of asthma are major risk factors for ARs. ADER also demonstrated that natural extracts were more likely to induce reactions than allergoids and identified an increased risk from birch and mugwort pollen extracts [ ]. Overall, the ADER concluded that SCIT is generally safe for adults with respiratory allergies, with most ARs being mild and severe events remaining rare. Modified allergens used in SCIT have been developed to improve safety by reducing the IgE-binding capacity while preserving immunogenicity and the ability to induce long-term immune tolerance. Among these, allergoids demonstrated a very favorable safety profile. Polymerized allergoids used in SCIT show extremely low rates of SRs, estimated at 0.0005–0.01% per injection [ ]. In addition, trials using high-dose grass pollen polymerized allergoids (e.g., aluminum-adsorbed preparations) have shown that intra-seasonal initiation of therapy does not increase SRs while still inducing robust immunological responses, such as increased allergen-specific IgG4 [ ]. Other engineered approaches, including recombinant allergens, peptides, and allergen–carrier fusion proteins, have demonstrated good safety profiles in clinical trials. For example, SCIT with recombinant Timothy grass allergens was well tolerated even at doses of up to 120 μg without major adverse effects, while peptide-based strategies and epitope-targeted vaccines aim to further minimize IgE-mediated reactions [ ]. 3.2. Sublingual Immunotherapy Safety SLIT is generally regarded as having a more favorable safety and tolerability profile than SCIT, offering a superior risk–benefit ratio largely because of fewer SARs, with no fatalities reported in clinical trials for SLIT tablets [ , , , , , , ]. Its safety profile permits at-home administration after the first dose is administered under medical supervision [ ]. The main ARs are LRs within the oral cavity—such as oral pruritus, throat irritation, and tongue edema. These reactions are typically mild-to-moderate in intensity, transient (often resolving within 30 min post-administration and usually within 2–4 weeks of starting treatment), and rarely lead to treatment discontinuation (in approximately 5% of patients) [ , , ]. For SLIT tablets, SARs are rare, with a large clinical trial database indicating an anaphylactic rate of 0.02% [ , , ]. US clinical trials of SLIT tablets have reported few SARs, and no serious events or airway compromise [ ]. Non-US studies have reported an SAR rate of 0.056% [ ]. The FDA requires an accompanying prescription for a self-injectable epinephrine autoinjector for SLIT tablets in the US; however, this is not a universal requirement in other countries. A history of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a contraindication for SLIT tablets, although a definitive causal link between SLIT tablets and EoE has yet to be established [ , ]. RWE reinforces this favorable safety profile. The REACT study reported one anaphylactic event in 3754 subjects treated with SLIT tablets. Similarly, the ADER registry, which evaluated 1060 SLIT courses, found that ARs were predominantly mild and severe events were rare. Overall, the extensive RWE confirmed that SLIT is generally safe and well-tolerated in adults and children with respiratory allergies. 4. Similarly, the ADER registry, which evaluated 1060 SLIT courses, found that ARs were predominantly mild and severe events were rare. Overall, the extensive RWE confirmed that SLIT is generally safe and well-tolerated in adults and children with respiratory allergies. 4. Conclusions AIT, delivered as SCIT or SLIT, remains the only established disease-modifying intervention for respiratory allergies to date, with convergent evidence from RCTs and RWE demonstrating consistent reductions in symptoms and medication use, along with improvements in QoL. Long-term follow-up data indicate that these benefits, if the treatment is maintained for at least 3 years, may persist beyond treatment discontinuation, suggesting sustained effects on disease progression. SCIT shows robust efficacy across AR/C but necessitates administration under medical supervision due to a higher, albeit infrequent, risk of SARs. SLIT provides efficacy while offering a more favorable safety profile dominated by transient LRs and a lower occurrence of SARs. Large RWE cohorts further support the effectiveness and safety of both SCIT and SLIT in routine clinical practice, broadening the evidence base to include diverse patient populations. Collectively, these findings underscore the role of AIT as a core element of respiratory allergy management. As there is no generic class effect on AIT efficacy and safety, treatment decisions should rely on product-specific evidence derived from clinical trials and real-world studies, in accordance with current guideline recommendations. Importantly, comparisons between SCIT and SLIT should not be interpreted as evidence of route-based superiority but rather as reflections of differences among individual products, study designs, and clinical contexts. Adherence and persistence are the key determinants of AIT effectiveness. Administration models differ substantially between SCIT, which is delivered under medical supervision in clinical settings, and SLIT, which is typically self-administered at home. While supervised administration may facilitate adherence monitoring and allow the direct verification of treatment persistence, home-based regimens rely more heavily on patient engagement, education, and long-term motivation. Real-world studies suggest that adherence to AIT can decline over time, particularly given the recommended multi-year treatment duration required to achieve sustained clinical benefits. These differences highlight the importance of structured follow-up strategies, digital adherence tools, and patient-centered education programs to support persistence in therapy. Therefore, optimizing adherence to routine practice is critical for translating the efficacy observed in clinical trials to long-term effectiveness in real-world populations. Integrating RWE with RCT data is essential to inform future guideline development, particularly for capturing long-term effects and real-world applicability.

Asthma is a chronic airway disease characterized by bronchial hyperreactivity, mucosal inflammation, and associated symptoms such as dyspnea, wheezing, cough, and mucus production [ ]. CRS is characterized by chronic nasal and paranasal sinus inflammation, with symptoms persisting for over 12 weeks. These include nasal congestion, discharge, facial pain, reduced sense of smell, and corroborative findings from endoscopy or computed tomography [ ]. CRS is a heterogeneous disease encompassing two main phenotypes: CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) and CRS without nasal polyps (CRSsNP). Immune responses are classified into T1, T2, and T3 pathways, each targeting specific classes of pathogens [ ]. T1 cytokines include IFN‐γ and IL‐12, T2 cytokines IL‐4, IL‐5, and IL‐13, and T3 cytokines IL‐17A and IL‐22 [ ]. These pathways are orchestrated by distinct innate lymphoid and T‐helper cell subsets, but inflammatory patterns are often mixed and highly plastic. In CRS and asthma, immune responses are chronic and polyclonal, triggered by multiple, partly unknown environmental factors [ ]. T2 inflammation is most commonly associated with allergic and non‐allergic eosinophilic asthma [ ], CRSwNP, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, eosinophilic CRS, central compartment atopic disease, and N‐ERD (NSAID‐exacerbated respiratory disease) [ ]. Although T2‐low asthma is less associated with CRS, T2‐low asthma endotypes (such as asthma‐COPD overlap syndrome, obesity‐related asthma, and pauci‐granulocytic asthma) can coexist with T2‐low CRSsNP sometimes alongside other T2‐low inflammatory disorders such as bronchiectasis [ ], primary ciliary dyskinesia, or cystic fibrosis [ ]. Asthma treatment aims to achieve symptomatic control through inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) for inflammation and, when necessary, bronchodilators. Additional therapies may be employed for persistent cases, such as long‐acting beta‐2 agonists, anticholinergics, leukotriene receptor antagonists, long‐term macrolide courses, or biologics [ ]. CRSwNP is more strongly associated with asthma and T2 inflammation than CRSsNP [ ]. Moreover, CRSwNP is linked to worse asthma control and severity. CRS treatment aims to disease control and typically involves intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) [ ]. After failure of baseline therapy, endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) may be considered. In addition, severe CRSwNP may be treated by oral corticosteroid (OCS) courses or biologics [ ]. Despite the frequent coexistence of CRSwNP and asthma, asthma often remains underdiagnosed in T2‐driven CRSwNP cases. Asthma comorbidity exacerbates CRS severity and complicates treatment, leading to increased rates of exacerbations and greater treatment resistance [ ]. Lower airway inflammation commonly accompanies CRS, with a substantial proportion of CRS patients also suffering from comorbid asthma [ ], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or bronchiectasis [ , ]. Notably, rhinitis/rhinosinusitis emerges as the most prevalent comorbidity of asthma [ ]. GINA 2025 guidelines advocate for thoroughly evaluating comorbidities, including CRS, at every stage of asthma treatment [ ]. Comorbid CRS and asthma lead to challenges in treatment balance, with increased rates of exacerbations and surgeries [ , , , , , , ] and thus lead to greater healthcare costs and reduced quality of life. Improved treatment approaches could mitigate these challenges. From an economic perspective, managing these comorbid conditions effectively minimizes productivity losses and absenteeism due to illness. The aim of the review is to evaluate current literature on risk factors of comorbid CRS and asthma and to highlight recent findings of treatment, such as biologics. This review represents the collective expert opinion of the Task Force, derived through a structured process that combined a systematic search of the literature with repeated rounds of internal discussion. A systematic literature review used the initial search phrase “chronic rhinosinusitis AND asthma.” Full‐text English articles were retrieved from the PubMed database, with the search limited to systematic reviews, meta‐analyses, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Exclusion criteria included studies not published in English, lack of available full texts, and studies where the abstract did not indicate the inclusion of subjects with both diseases. A systematic literature review used the initial search phrase “chronic rhinosinusitis AND asthma.” Full‐text English articles were retrieved from the PubMed database, with the search limited to systematic reviews, meta‐analyses, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Exclusion criteria included studies not published in English, lack of available full texts, and studies where the abstract did not indicate the inclusion of subjects with both diseases. Clinical trials, meta‐analyses, and other studies have been referred out of the search, if needed. 2 Risk Factors for Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Risk factors for the development of comorbid asthma in patients with CRSwNP include female sex, a history of allergic rhinitis, elevated serum total IgE levels, and increased blood eosinophil counts [ ]. Comorbid CRS and asthma share overlapping pathophysiological mechanisms as well as genetic predispositions. This chapter highlights only selected examples, as the underlying immunological and pathophysiological mechanisms have been discussed in detail in other task force reports [ ]. 2.1 Shared Pathomechanisms Pathogenesis of both CRS and asthma is related to genetic predisposition, dysbiosis and aberrant host‐barrier interactions [ ]. Accordingly, their shared pathomechanisms likely reflect overlapping genetic susceptibility, microbiota alterations, environmental exposures, and host responses related to common airway anatomy, immune pathways, and neural innervation [ ]. Patients with CRS and/or asthma have shown to exhibit a reduced biodiversity [ , ]. Staphylococcus aureus colonization, among others, has been shown to be associated with increased asthma prevalence in both CRSwNP and CRSsNP patients [ , ]. Dysfunction of the airway barrier, as observed in rhinitis and CRS, facilitates the passage of exogenous particles, including allergens, thereby promoting inflammation that spans both the upper and lower airways [ ]. The interplay between systemic and neurogenic inflammatory mechanisms in the naso‐bronchial axis, along with the integrity of airway epithelial barriers, is increasingly recognized as critical in linking upper and lower airway disease [ , , ]. Most patients with comorbid CRS and asthma show shared T2‐dominated inflammatory pathways [ , , ] (Figure ), which underpin the effectiveness of biologics. Recent data indicate that IL‐5, along with IL‐4 and IL‐13, plays a crucial role in predicting comorbid asthma in patients with CRSwNP [ ]. As our understanding of chronic upper and lower airway disease pathophysiology deepens, the case for targeted therapies that address the underlying immune mechanisms of both conditions becomes increasingly compelling [ ]. 2.2 Genetic Predisposition Genome‐wide analysis in FinnGen and UK Biobank has identified extensive shared genetic architecture between asthma and CRSwNP, with 71 loci jointly associated and enrichment of pathways related to type 2 inflammation, JAK–STAT , and FOXP3 signaling [ ]. The same group identified 41 genetic loci associated with inflammatory and infectious upper respiratory diseases, including 12 novel loci, and demonstrated a genetic link between asthma and IURDs [ ]. In the United States, a study conducted at Geisinger examined 483 European Americans with at least two of six CRS symptoms persisting over 3 months [ ]. The control group comprised 2057 individuals without CRS, nasal polyps (NP), asthma, allergic rhinitis, or sinus abnormalities (confirmed by CT scans or endoscopy). Genotype analysis revealed two loci potentially linked to CRS, emphasizing the upper respiratory tract's role in disease development. Additionally, a meta‐analysis by Kristjansson et al. [ ] identified iIL‐21 upregulation as a key factor in CRS/NP pathogenesis. A bioinformatics study investigating allergic CRS with NP (ACRSwNP) utilized datasets ( GSE23552 , GSE104468 , and GSE41861 ) to identify differentially expressed genes associated with ACRSwNP. CST1 emerged as a critical gene highly expressed in the nasal and bronchial mucosa of ACRSwNP patients. This gene was linked to type 2 inflammation, as evidenced by elevated CST1 and IL5RA levels in ACRSwNP patients [ ]. Of the 2739 CRS cases, 50.33% also had asthma, 4.9% had Samter's triad, and 4.28% had eosinophilia. The review highlighted significant SNPs associated with CRS and emphasized the need for further genetic studies [ ]. A meta‐analysis of biobank data studies from the UK and Iceland identified significant genetic loci associated with CRS and NP [ ]. For NP, 10 loci were identified (e.g., ALOX15 , HLA , IL33 ), with two loci ( ALOX15 , HLA ) shared between CRS and NP. Studies like the HELIUS study have linked CRS with adult‐onset asthma [ ], while the Asthma Clinical Research Network has shown CRS to heighten the risk of asthma exacerbations [ ]. In cases where asthma patients also have CRS, acute exacerbations of CRS often result in suboptimal asthma control [ ]. Up to two‐thirds of CRS patients have asthma [ ], while 40% to 75% of asthma patients have comorbid CRS. In a randomized clinical trial of patients with severe CRSwNP, 79% had comorbid asthma. Among these patients, 58% had uncontrolled asthma, and 22% represented newly diagnosed asthma cases [ ]. Although direct causality between the two conditions has not been established, there is a clear correlation between the severity of CRS and the severity of asthma [ ]. Both CRS and asthma contribute to upper and lower airway symptoms and affect overall disease control, making it difficult to determine which condition drives specific symptoms. Even in CRS patients who do not explicitly report bronchial symptoms, pulmonary function is notably impaired compared to non‐CRS individuals [ ]. The magnitude of the effect of comorbidities on asthma outcomes has shown to be clinically important [ ]. Patients with comorbid CRSwNP and asthma present overtreatment of asthma using high‐dose ICS and poor asthma control, with up to 10% of patients experiencing severe exacerbations, impaired lung function, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare costs, despite the use of high doses of OCS [ ]. Registry data from the Severe Asthma Network in Italy show that patients with severe asthma and CRSwNP experience worse outcomes, including more frequent exacerbations, prolonged OCS use, and a higher likelihood of requiring long‐term OCS, compared to severe asthma patients without CRSwNP [ ]. Moreover, patients with severe asthma and comorbid CRSwNP experience worse outcomes, including more frequent exacerbations, longer use of OCS, and a higher likelihood of needing long‐term OCS, compared to those with severe asthma without CRSwNP. Assessing asthma's effect on CRS is complicated by reliance on patient‐reported diagnoses, variable outcome measures, and heterogeneity in endotypes and phenotypes. Some studies report higher symptom scores, such as the SNOT‐22 in asthmatics [ , ], while others, such as a Croatian cohort of 250 CRS patients (26% with asthma), found no significant differences except for lower VAS scores for smell, likely reflecting the T2‐high inflammatory endotype [ ]. Other studies suggest that CRS may exert a more pronounced impact on asthma control than vice versa [ ]. Taken together, although the upper and lower airways influence each other, studies suggest that CRS has a greater impact on asthma symptoms than vice versa. As a result, pulmonologists, allergists, and pediatricians may more readily refer patients to otorhinolaryngologists. In contrast, the impact of asthma on CRS symptoms may be less evident, potentially delaying asthma diagnosis and control in otorhinolaryngology clinics. Moreover, limited access to or familiarity with lung function testing may further complicate asthma assessment in otorhinolaryngology clinics, underscoring the importance of considering consultation even in the absence of overt asthma symptoms. 4 Treatment Implications Comorbid CRS and asthma represent a significant therapeutic challenge, as a substantial proportion of affected patients are difficult to treat. This comorbidity is associated with high‐dose ICS use, poor control of both asthma and CRS, frequent exacerbations, repeated OCS courses, recurrent surgeries, impaired lung function, and reduced QoL [ , ]. Accordingly, the latter part of this review focuses on the impact of current treatment strategies on comorbid CRS and asthma and discusses biologic therapies for comorbid CRS and asthma (Figures and ). Baseline treatment for comorbid CRS and asthma includes intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) and inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), supplemented by anticholinergics, nasal irrigation, inhaled short‐acting beta agonists (SABA) or long‐acting beta‐agonists (LABA), long‐acting muscarine antagonists (LAMA), and leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) [ , ]. Antibiotics are prescribed when there is evidence of bacterial infection. Systemic corticosteroids, which are potent anti‐inflammatory agents, may be used in short courses for exacerbations of asthma or CRSwNP. However, systemic corticosteroids are associated with a range of side effects and increased mortality, which are linked to their cumulative dosage [ , ]. ESS is considered when conservative management fails. There is limited knowledge of the optimal timing and extent of ESS.

In general, biologics are considered for patients with severe disease who continue to have significant symptoms despite maximal baseline therapy, frequent OCS use, and—when applicable—ESS for CRSwNP [ , , ]. 4.1 Impact of Intranasal or Inhaled Corticosteroids on Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma There is limited knowledge of the impact of ICS on CRS in patients with comorbid CRS and asthma. Greiff et al. investigated the use of ICS in non‐asthmatic allergic rhinitis patients during the pollen season. They observed reduced eosinophil levels in blood and nasal tissues and decreased seasonal nasal symptoms in patients treated with inhaled budesonide [ ]. There is some evidence of the impact of INCS on asthma in patients with comorbid CRS and asthma. In a 16‐week single‐center study, Stelmach et al. [ ] demonstrated that INCS treatment in patients with allergic rhinitis and asthma reduced pulmonary symptoms, with intranasal budesonide (400 mcg) proving as effective as inhaled budesonide (1000 mcg) or a combination of both. However, the absence of a placebo group limits the generalizability of these findings. A 24‐week multicenter, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled randomized clinical trial (RCT) by Dixon et al. [ ] further explored the impact of intranasal mometasone in 388 patients with uncontrolled asthma and chronic rhinitis or sinusitis. While the treatment modestly reduced asthma and sinus symptom scores, it did not significantly improve lung function, asthma quality of life, or rates of poorly controlled asthma, highlighting the limitations of INCS in asthma management. In contrast, a large retrospective study by Adams et al. [ ] involving 13,844 asthma patients demonstrated that INCS therapy reduced the risk of emergency department visits, independent of inhaled corticosteroid use. This underscores the potential systemic benefits of INCS beyond their local effects on sinonasal disease. In addition, studies exist on the effect of INCS in patients with comorbid rhinitis and asthma. A Cochrane meta‐analysis suggests that intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) indirectly control asthma through the management of rhinitis. However, the analysis failed to demonstrate significant improvements in asthma symptoms or lung function [ ]. Corren et al. reported that INCS prevented increased bronchial responsiveness associated with seasonal pollen exposure in allergic rhinitis patients with asthma [ ]. In non‐asthmatic children with allergic rhinitis, INCS significantly reduced airway hyperresponsiveness to methacholine but did not affect asthma symptoms [ ]. Dahl et al. [ ] found no effect of 6 weeks of INCS on airway reactivity or induced sputum eosinophilia. Katial et al. [ ] and Nathan et al. [ ] found that 4 weeks of INCS improved nasal symptoms but had no effect on asthma control. Together, short‐term INCS use appears to have a limited impact on asthma outcomes, while longer‐term studies show modest benefits, primarily in symptom reduction rather than lung function or asthma control. Further prospective and controlled studies are needed to elucidate the full potential of INCS and ICS in the context of comorbid CRS and asthma. 4.2 Impact of Systemic Corticosteroids on <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Systemic corticosteroids (SCS) carry significant side effects, requiring careful consideration of their risks versus benefits. Short courses of SCS have proven their effect for acute exacerbations of asthma. In CRSwNP, OCS effectively reduce polyp size, improve olfaction, and alleviate symptoms; however, their effects are short‐lived [ ]. OCS are not recommended for CRSsNP. One study reported that nearly 17% of patients with asthma were prescribed OCS specifically for CRS comorbidity [ ]. A prospective study of 108 asthmatic CRS patients found that CRS exacerbations requiring OCS were significantly associated with poorer asthma control (ACT score) [ ]. Repeated upper airway–related OCS courses may therefore signal uncontrolled asthma. Only few studies have directly evaluated the impact of OCS on outcome of comorbid CRS and asthma. A cohort study by Epperson et al. followed 64 CRS patients treated with a 15‐day prednisone taper plus INCS. Over 2–5 months, patients with comorbid asthma showed less improvement in SNOT‐22 scores than non‐asthmatic CRS patients; however, the absence of a control group limits interpretation [ ]. Over 2–5 months, patients with comorbid asthma showed less improvement in SNOT‐22 scores than non‐asthmatic CRS patients; however, the absence of a control group limits interpretation [ ]. A Chinese prospective study compared oral methylprednisolone, budesonide transnasal nebulization, and budesonide nasal spray in 91 eosinophilic CRSwNP patients, including 17 with asthma. However, the timing and rationale for OCS use were not reported. In the prospective cross‐sectional study of 110 asthmatics by Philips et al., it was found that higher SNOT‐22 scores predicted the need for asthma‐related OCS. However, the SNOT‐22 questionnaire also includes items influenced by asthma symptoms, such as cough and fatigue, potentially confounding results [ ]. An American case–control study comparing 637 asthmatics with CRS to 637 controls without CRS found no difference in asthma‐related OCS use between the groups (15.3% vs. 14.6%) [ ]. Current evidence is insufficient to make definitive recommendations on SCS use in patients with comorbid CRS and asthma. Given the well‐documented side effects, the dose, duration, and number of SCS courses should be minimized while maintaining control during exacerbations. Repeated upper airway–related OCS courses may indicate uncontrolled asthma, and vice versa, highlighting the need for multidisciplinary management. 4.3 Impact of Endoscopic Sinus Surgery on Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma ESS is an option for CRS patients who do not achieve adequate control with medical therapy [ ]. Its primary goal is to restore nasal and sinus ventilation and drainage, supporting normal mucosal functions, as seen in procedures like the Draf approach. Modern endoscopic techniques minimize tissue resection while preserving surrounding structures [ ]. While ESS benefits are well documented, the additional value of extended ESS for disease control and QoL remains debated [ , ]. ESS improves sinonasal function, reduces inflammatory edema and polyps, and provides better disease control than medical therapy alone [ ]. ESS improves SNOT‐22 scores [ ], and because some items capture lower airway burden, these changes may also reflect systemic airway involvement and improvement. Nevertheless, studies report both positive and negative effects of comorbid asthma on SNOT‐22 improvement after ESS [ , , ]. A meta‐analysis of 15 studies including 3048 patients found that ESS improved SNOT‐22 scores by an average of 23 points, well above the MCID of 8.9. Comorbid CRS and asthma were associated with greater improvements [ ]. In patients with comorbid CRS and asthma, ESS has shown to improve asthma. Although ESS does not directly target the lower airways, it can benefit asthmatics by reducing post‐nasal drip, improving nasal airflow, and enhancing sleep and overall respiratory function, which may improve asthma control [ ]. A meta‐analysis of 22 studies (mean follow‐up 26.4 months) [ ] reported improvements in overall asthma control (76.1%), as well as reduction of asthma attacks (84.8%), hospitalizations (64.4%), and emergency visits (> 90% in two studies) [ , ]. Postoperatively, the fraction of patients with controlled asthma increased by 12% to 83%, while OCS use decreased in 72.8% of patients; ICS and bronchodilator use also declined (28.5% and 36.3%, respectively). Mean FEV1 improvement (1.62%) was not statistically significant. Benefits were particularly notable in severe asthma. In a 21‐week study of 68 patients with asthma and nasal polyposis, FESS significantly improved asthma symptom scores, daily PEFR, and nasal parameters [ ]. Long‐term outcomes of ESS depend on CRS endotype [ , , ]. Comorbid CRSwNP and asthma have been linked to higher rates of postoperative polyp recurrence (up to 80% of patients within 18 months) [ ] and a two‐fold risk for revision surgery (up to 40%–50% of patients within 3–5 years) [ , , ]. Higher revision rates were linked to asthma (22.6%), allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (28.7%), N‐ERD (27.2%), and prior polypectomy (26%), while only 8% of patients without asthma required revision [ ]. In patients with the most severe disease—such as those with comorbid CRSwNP and N‐ERD—the clinical benefits of ESS are often short‐lived, with polyp recurrence and symptom relapse typically occurring within 1–2 years postoperatively [ ]. As a result, individuals with coexisting CRSwNP and asthma commonly undergo multiple revision surgeries, leading to accumulating procedural risk and healthcare utilization. Optimal asthma control is essential prior to ESS performed under general anesthesia. Comprehensive evidence is lacking on both the direct and indirect costs and risks of extensive ESS in this patient population, as well as its impact on overall healthcare utilization. Taken together, ESS has limited potential alone for long‐term control of severe T2‐high airway inflammation and underscores the need to consider such as biologic therapies. 4.4 Impact of Long‐Term Macrolides on Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Macrolides have been studied separately in asthma or in CRS [ ] in several clinical trials. A systematic meta‐analysis studied 17 reports with macrolide treatment durations ranging from 6 to 48 weeks in the management of adult patients with asthma [ ]. Another meta‐analysis studied 7 reports and showed that macrolides did not significantly reduce asthma exacerbations compared with placebo but modestly reduced rescue SABA use, with no increase in serious adverse events [ ]. Overall, macrolides have a limited role, likely reserved for steroid‐resistant asthmatics or patients who are ineligible for, have limited access to, or derive insufficient benefit from biologics. Among CRS patients, a meta‐analysis of eight studies ( n = 606) found that long‐term macrolide therapy provided no significant benefit for SNOT or VAS scores, modestly improved postoperative nasal endoscopic score, and did not increase adverse events [ ]. Overall, macrolides had limited impact on quality of life or CRS severity, and evidence was insufficient to assess phenotype‐ or race‐specific effects. Together, current evidence is insufficient to recommend use of long‐term macrolides in the management of CRS. Macrolides may offer only marginal benefit in adult asthma. To date, there is no evidence of macrolides on co‐morbid CRS and asthma. 4.5 Impact of Allergen Immunotherapy on Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) is an effective immunity‐modifying treatment for allergic rhinitis with or without allergic asthma [ ]. Exhaled nitric oxide and eosinophil levels, when interpreted within the clinical context, may serve as surrogate biomarkers of treatment response. There is limited knowledge of the impact of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) on comorbid CRS and asthma [ ]. AIT may serve as an adjunctive treatment in patients with CRSwNP, potentially improving symptoms and surgical outcomes [ ]. However, due to limited evidence, there is little support for its use in CRSsNP, and no studies have evaluated sublingual immunotherapy in this patient population. 4.6 Impact of Biologics on Comorbid <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Several monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are currently approved or under active investigation for treating severe uncontrolled asthma or severe CRSwNP [ ] (Figure , Table ). Biologic therapy for severe asthma is guided by phenotypes and biomarkers, whereas biologic use in severe CRSwNP is less restricted without current reliance on biomarker‐based guidance [ ]. Several biologics have been approved or have shown effect or are under investigation for children [ ]. The effect of biologics is also under investigation for CRSsNP. Benralizumab and reslizumab have not proven their effect in CRSwNP. Dupilumab targets the alpha chain of the IL‐4 receptor, thereby inhibiting both IL‐4 and IL‐13 signaling [ ]. The approved indications of these biologics have expanded to include several chronic inflammatory diseases. In brief, Omalizumab is approved by both FDA and EMA for moderate‐to‐severe persistent allergic asthma, CRSwNP, and chronic spontaneous urticaria, and additionally by the FDA for IgE‐mediated food allergy. Mepolizumab is approved by both the FDA and EMA for severe asthma, CRSwNP, hypereosinophilic syndrome, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and by the FDA only for COPD. Depemokimab is FDA‐approved for severe asthma but not yet for severe CRSwNP. Dupilumab is approved by both agencies for moderate‐to‐severe atopic dermatitis, severe type 2 asthma, severe CRSwNP, prurigo nodularis, eosinophilic esophagitis, and moderate‐to‐severe spontaneous urticaria. It is FDA‐approved and under EMA review for bullous pemphigoid, and under FDA priority review for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis. Tezepelumab is approved by the FDA and EMA for severe asthma and severe CRSwNP [ ], but not yet for severe COPD [ ]. Benralizumab is approved by both the FDA and EMA for severe eosinophilic asthma and by the FDA only for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). Reslizumab is approved solely for severe asthma, and its intravenous dosing limits its practical use (Table ). CRSwNP is frequently associated with eosinophilic asthma [ ], and its endotypic diversity is less pronounced compared to that of severe asthma [ ]. Pivotal trials of biologics primarily focus on the specific disease of the recruited population [ , , , , , , , , , ]. Since approximately 80% of patients with severe CRSwNP also have asthma, and 40% of patients with eosinophilic severe asthma have comorbid CRSwNP [ ], it is possible to stratify clinical trial data to focus on this subgroup. Indeed, numerous post hoc analyses of phase III trials have demonstrated the efficacy of biologics in patients with comorbid CRS and asthma [ , , , , , , , ]. However, to the authors' knowledge, there are no clinical trials focusing solely on comorbid CRS and asthma phenotype. A clinical trial has shown that dupilumab is superior to omalizumab in patients with severe CRSwNP and coexisting asthma [ , ]. All mAbs approved for severe asthma have been shown to reduce annualized exacerbation rates, improve asthma control, and enhance quality of life (QoL) [ , , ]. They also positively impact lung function, though the observed increase in FEV1 may not always surpass the minimal clinically important difference. Moreover, mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab, and dupilumab have demonstrated the ability to reduce the maintenance dose of OCS. While no direct head‐to‐head comparisons exist, available evidence suggests that these biologics likely exhibit phenotype‐specific efficacy. The four biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, dupilumab, and tezepelumab) approved for CRSwNP have demonstrated efficacy in improving QoL, reducing the nasal polyp score (NPS) and nasal blockage, and decreasing the need for ESS [ , , , ]. In this population, up to 94% of patients showed an excellent‐to‐moderate response to the sinonasal disease, according to EPOS [ ]. Moreover, the severity of CRSwNP and the blood eosinophil count were associated with a better response in both the upper and lower airways, especially in N‐ERD patients [ ]. Of note is that patients with comorbid CRSwNP and N‐ERD showed a higher improvement of health‐related QoL than subjects suffering from CRSwNP only [ ]. A study analyzing the effect of switching to dupilumab in 20 comorbid patients who showed good asthma control but insufficient CRSwNP control with other biologicals reported a general improvement of sinonasal outcomes, with only one individual experiencing worsening asthma symptoms [ ]. The five studies investigating the effect of mepolizumab in comorbid individuals include mainly high eosinophilic patients [ , , , , ]. Mepolizumab induced a higher reduction of CRSwNP exacerbations, all‐cause OCS intake, and ESS requirements in asthmatic individuals compared to patients with CRSwNP only over a year of treatment [ ]. Moreover, the presence of CRSwNP identified the individuals with eosinophilic severe asthma, achieving a greater improvement of their asthma parameters by mepolizumab in a real‐life study [ ]. Seven works analyzed the performance of omalizumab in patients with CRSwNP and severe asthma [ , , , , , , ]. In an observational study, omalizumab improved asthma parameters comparably in allergic subjects with and without CRSwNP [ ]. Similarly, allergic status or asthma presence did not affect omalizumab‐induced improvement of CRSwNP in a post hoc analysis of several clinical trials [ ]. Interestingly, the mechanism of action of omalizumab might be affected by the presence of upper airway disease. Despite similar clinical benefits, only asthma patients without concomitant CRSwNP showed significantly reduced serum periostin during omalizumab therapy [ ]. The six real‐life studies and post hoc analyses published to date with blood eosinophilia in eosinophilic severe asthma consistently show that CRSwNP patients' asthma outcomes improve more than in subjects without sinonasal disease [ , , , , , ]. A post hoc analysis of a clinical trial of reslizumab for eosinophilic severe asthma also demonstrated a higher improvement of asthma parameters in comorbid individuals [ ]. In addition to improving lung function and asthma control and reducing the number of exacerbations, tezepelumab improved sinonasal symptoms in patients with severe asthma and CRSwNP [ ]. Meta‐analyses and indirect comparisons in patients with severe uncontrolled asthma show no significant differences in efficacy—based on exacerbation rates, ACQ scores, or FEV1—between anti‐TSLP, anti‐IL5/5Rα, anti‐IL4Rα, and anti‐IgE therapies, except that tezepelumab may reduce exacerbations better than benralizumab [ ]. Meta‐analyses suggest that dupilumab and tezepelumab may offer greater benefits than other biologics in certain efficacy outcomes [ , , , ]. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution, as differences in baseline disease severity and prior ESS history among study populations may confound comparisons [ ]. Furthermore, meta‐analyses provide limited evidence for the newest biologics. To date, no validated guidelines exist on strategic selection of biologics or switching of them for comorbid CRS and asthma. Endotyping for respiratory biologic selection remains in early stages and requires further investigation. Patient comorbidities and specific laboratory findings may inform biologic selection; for instance, when a patient has multiple indications such as atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic esophagitis, or chronic urticaria, the secondary indication can guide therapy choice [ ]. Dupilumab, tezepelumab, depemokimab, and mepolizumab may offer the greatest dual benefit for upper and lower airway diseases in comorbid patients. Omalizumab's efficacy remains in patients with comorbid allergic asthma. If uncontrolled after one biologic, early switching of biologics may result in better clinical outcomes [ ]. Switching biologics in patients with comorbid severe asthma and CRS should be guided by endotype, and switching between biologics in the same class is generally not recommended [ ]. For example, if blood eosinophil levels rise, the patient may benefit from switching from dupilumab to mepolizumab or to tezepelumab. Similarly, if exhaled nitric oxide increases, indicating heightened mucosal eosinophilia, a switch from dupilumab to mepolizumab or to tezepelumab may also be advantageous. There is little evidence (case reports or small series) on the effect of dual biologics in severe asthma or severe CRSwNP [ ], yet it has not been studied in clinical trials nor in patients with comorbid severe asthma and CRS. 5 Treatment of Patients With Comorbid N‐<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ERD</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug (NSAID)‐exacerbated respiratory disease (N‐ERD) is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder affecting patients with asthma and/or CRS (wNP), with symptoms triggered by NSAID exposure [ ]. Dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism and overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes are key pathophysiological mechanisms driving inflammation in this subset [ ]. N‐ERD occurs in approximately 5%–12% of adults with asthma, up to 15% of those with severe asthma, and around 9% of patients with CRSwNP [ , , ]. N‐ERD, CRSwNP, and asthma often form a difficult‐to‐treat triad characterized by poor symptom control, frequent exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids, high healthcare utilization, and repeated sinus surgeries [ , ]. On the other hand, a Spanish study assessing general quality of life using the SF‐36 questionnaire found that while the presence of nasal polyps and asthma significantly impaired quality of life, the additional presence of N‐ERD did not [ ]. Standard care of N‐ERD focuses on optimizing asthma and CRS control with corticosteroids, bronchodilators, saline irrigation [ ], and short courses of OCS for exacerbations [ , ]. N‐ERD is often severe and challenging to treat, and persistent disease reflects T2‐high inflammation [ , ], underscoring the potential of biologics as a key treatment strategy [ ]. Relapse rates of surgery are high among N‐ERD patients with CRSwNP [ , ]. Aspirin therapy after desensitization (ATAD) shows inconsistent benefit to CRSwNP and may cause adverse effects such as asthma worsening, bleeding, and gastrointestinal harm [ , , ]. Therefore, biologic therapies have emerged as promising options. 5.1 Impact of Biologics on Patients With Comorbid N‐<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ERD</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Studies have investigated the effect of biologics in patients with severe asthma, CRS, and N‐ERD (Table ). Post hoc analyses of clinical phase III trials have shown that dupilumab, mepolizumab, and tezepelumab are effective in patients with comorbid N‐ERD [ , , ]. There are lacking phase IV clinical trials directly observing patients with N‐ERD with severe CRSwNP or severe asthma. A retrospective study of 74 patients with N‐ERD [ ] examined the impact of biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab, and dupilumab) on symptoms, SNOT‐22 scores, corticosteroid and antibiotic use, and emergency visits. Of the 74, 49 patients continued dupilumab treatment, with 85% reporting symptom improvement. In contrast, 48.6% of omalizumab users and 26.9% of those on other biologics reported improvements. Dupilumab patients also showed significant improvements in SNOT‐22 scores and

tezepelumab are effective in patients with comorbid N‐ERD [ , , ]. There are lacking phase IV clinical trials directly observing patients with N‐ERD with severe CRSwNP or severe asthma. A retrospective study of 74 patients with N‐ERD [ ] examined the impact of biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab, and dupilumab) on symptoms, SNOT‐22 scores, corticosteroid and antibiotic use, and emergency visits. Of the 74, 49 patients continued dupilumab treatment, with 85% reporting symptom improvement. In contrast, 48.6% of omalizumab users and 26.9% of those on other biologics reported improvements. Dupilumab patients also showed significant improvements in SNOT‐22 scores and a reduction in corticosteroid and antibiotic use, while other biologics showed no significant differences. The study concluded that dupilumab provided the most significant clinical improvement in N‐ERD patients. A retrospective study conducted by Ghiasi et al. [ ] analyzed the impact of biological therapies on systemic corticosteroid use in 74 patients with N‐ERD. Of the 32 patients treated with biologics for at least 1 year, the median cumulative corticosteroid exposure decreased significantly from 215 mg to −178.2 mg after 1 year. Dupilumab, the most commonly prescribed biologic, showed a significant reduction of −156.3 mg, while omalizumab had a median reduction of −300 mg. However, data for benralizumab and mepolizumab were insufficient for statistical analysis. The study concluded that biologics significantly reduce corticosteroid use in N‐ERD patients, potentially decreasing long‐term corticosteroid‐associated complications. Despite the positive results, the study's sample size. A retrospective study [ ] evaluated biologics for asthma in 64 patients, 55 of whom had CRS, including 13 with N‐ERD and mostly CRSwNP. Biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab) improved nasal polyp scores, SNOT‐22, reduced systemic corticosteroid use, and halved ENT visits. Patients with N‐ERD had higher dropout rates and were more likely to require surgery, likely reflecting more severe disease. 5.2 Studies on Surgery or <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ATAD</styled-content> in Patients With Comorbid N‐<styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ERD</styled-content>, <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CRS</styled-content> and Asthma Treatment of N‐ERD with CRSwNP involves a complex interplay between ESS, ATAD, and biologics. Studies comparing surgery, ATAD, and biologics are scarce and only retrospective. Hence, evidence‐based guidelines defining the optimal therapeutic strategy of N‐ERD are currently lacking. There are few prospective controlled studies focusing on comparison between ASA and placebo and they have been performed with a small number of patients. A Polish study group randomized 20 N‐ERD and 14 CRSwNP patients to receive 624 mg of ASA or placebo, with follow‐ups conducted monthly over 6 months [ ]. Improvements in SNOT‐22 scores, nasal peak inspiratory flow, and reduced corticosteroid use were observed only in the N‐ERD group who received ASA. However, no significant changes in peak expiratory flow (PEF) or FEV1 values were noted. Four patients discontinued desensitization due to side effects. An Iranian study group randomized 34 N‐ERD patients to receive ASA ( n = 18) or placebo ( n = 16) [ ]. Patients in the ASA group received 650 mg of ASA twice daily for 1 month, followed by 325 mg twice daily for 6 months. The ASA group showed significant reductions in symptom scores (7.5 vs. 10.6) and corticosteroid use (9.3 vs. 11.0) compared to the placebo group. FEV1 improved more in the desensitization group (87.1 vs. 80.1), and Lund‐Mackay scores decreased significantly (11.1 vs. 15.1). Two patients discontinued due to side effects [ ]. Finnish study group randomized 26 N‐ERD patients to receive ASA ( n = 16) or placebo ( n = 10) [ ]. The ASA group received 125 mg ASA daily for 1 month, followed by 250 mg daily for 10 months. No difference between placebo and ATAD was detected for SNOT‐22, ACT, nasal polyp score, or need for OCS courses. Three patients from the ASA arm and one from the placebo arm discontinued due to adverse events. Together, these studies suggest that the use of ATAD is limited by the difficulty in predicting side effects and efficacy among N‐ERD patients. Retrospective cohort data exist comparing ATAD, surgery or biologics among N‐ERD patients. A US cohort study involving 98 patients at a specialized N‐ERD clinic assessed the effectiveness of ATAD and biologics, with most patients undergoing or being offered ATAD [ ]. Approximately 78% of patients continued daily aspirin therapy for nearly 4 years, with 75% reporting it as effective. A subset of 24 patients who received biologics in addition to ATAD represented those who tolerated aspirin but remained symptomatic, indicating a need to identify features favoring biologic therapy. The study concluded that ATAD provides a definitive disease‐modifying effect for a significant minority, while biologics address residual symptoms in others [ ]. Workman and Breuer highlighted the significant burden of N‐ERD on patients' quality of life, financial situation, and mental health, noting the high prevalence of depression and sleep disturbances. The study concluded that ATAD provides a definitive disease‐modifying effect for a significant minority, while biologics address residual symptoms in others [ ]. Workman and Breuer highlighted the significant burden of N‐ERD on patients' quality of life, financial situation, and mental health, noting the high prevalence of depression and sleep disturbances. These patients often require repeated medical and surgical interventions, including ESS. While biologics offer an alternative therapeutic approach, their continuous use is necessary to prevent disease recurrence, making them substantially more expensive than traditional pharmacological or surgical treatments [ ]. A US retrospective study (2011–2021) further examined the comparative efficacy of biologics and ATAD in 43N‐ERD patients, identifying asthma, CRSwNP, and N‐ERD as inclusion criteria [ ]. Among the participants, 45.7% received biologics (omalizumab, dupilumab, mepolizumab, or benralizumab), and 54.5% underwent ATAD. The study demonstrated that biologics led to superior improvements in Meltzer polyp scores (82% reduction), SNOT‐22 scores (nearly halved), and asthma control test (ACT) scores (improving from 15.2 to 20.42 within 6 months). Additionally, a 42% decrease in exhaled nitric oxide (FENO) suggested that biologics effectively target lower airway inflammation compared to ATAD. Overall, biologics yielded greater benefits in nasal and sinus symptoms and asthma control. Expert reviews by Laidlaw et al. [ ], Xu et al. [ ], and Buchheit et al. [ ], further refined the therapeutic strategy for N‐ERD. Laidlaw et al. recommended sinus surgery followed by ATAD as the initial approach for younger patients with well‐controlled asthma and a primary focus on preventing polyp regrowth, whereas biologics were advised for patients with severe asthma, a history of gastritis, or bleeding risk. Xu et al. emphasized the cost‐effectiveness of starting with surgery and ATAD, reserving dupilumab for refractory cases, and noted that dupilumab significantly improves nasal polyp scores and sense of smell. Buchheit et al. acknowledged the advancements biologics represent for T2‐high inflammatory diseases, including N‐ERD, but stressed their high costs, limited long‐term safety data, and the necessity of prior ESS and ATAD in most cases. They underscored the importance of individualized treatment strategies and further research to optimize biological selection [ , , ]. In conclusion, while biologics provide substantial benefits in symptom control and inflammation reduction for N‐ERD patients, their role is best considered within a comprehensive treatment plan that includes ESS and ATAD for appropriate candidates. Further studies are needed to refine treatment algorithms and identify patient populations that benefit most from biologics. 6 Conclusions and Future Research Needs The burden of comorbid CRS and asthma is substantial, as these patients are frequently underdiagnosed and undertreated, or present with severe, progressive disease. This population therefore requires dedicated clinical guidelines tailored to this specific phenotype, as well as a structured multidisciplinary approach to management involving otorhinolaryngologists, pulmonologists, allergists, and, when appropriate, pediatricians and immunologists. The coexistence of CRS and asthma—particularly in severe phenotypes such as CRSwNP and/or N‐ERD—represents a multifaceted clinical challenge that underscores the close interconnection between the upper and lower airways. Shared inflammatory pathways support the “united airways” concept and emphasize the need for integrated, comprehensive management strategies (Figure ). Advances in biologics, ESS, and ATAD have substantially improved outcomes in this patient population; however, treatment responses remain heterogeneous and difficult to predict. ESS significantly improves sinonasal outcomes and may also lead to modest improvements in asthma symptoms and need for OCS courses. More extensive surgical approaches may offer superior short‐term outcomes but are associated with increased risks and costs. In the most severe cases—often involving comorbid CRSwNP and N‐ERD—the benefits of ESS are frequently transient, with polyp regrowth and symptom recurrence occurring within 1–2 years after surgery. Consequently, patients with comorbid CRSwNP and asthma often require repeated surgeries, increasing cumulative surgical risk and healthcare burden. Asthma must be well‐controlled before surgery in general anesthesia. Numerous post hoc analyses of clinical trials and real‐world studies demonstrate that dupilumab, tezepelumab, mepolizumab, and depemokimab are effective and safe in patients with comorbid CRS and asthma. Dupilumab, mepolizumab, depemokimab, and omalizumab have emerged as transformative therapies, particularly in patients with severe T2 inflammation. Tezepelumab has shown efficacy in both T2‐high and T2‐low asthma and in CRSwNP, while itepekimab has demonstrated efficacy in asthma and is currently under investigation for CRSwNP. Mepolizumab, dupilumab, and tezepelumab have also shown benefit in patients with comorbid N‐ERD. Meta‐analyses suggest that dupilumab and tezepelumab may be the most potent biologics for severe CRSwNP; however, the limited number of meta‐analyses, different inclusion criteria of the RCTs, and the scarcity of data on newer biologics constrain the strength of this evidence. Depemokimab is a promising emerging therapy with extended dosing intervals

transformative therapies, particularly in patients with severe T2 inflammation. Tezepelumab has shown efficacy in both T2‐high and T2‐low asthma and in CRSwNP, while itepekimab has demonstrated efficacy in asthma and is currently under investigation for CRSwNP. Mepolizumab, dupilumab, and tezepelumab have also shown benefit in patients with comorbid N‐ERD. Meta‐analyses suggest that dupilumab and tezepelumab may be the most potent biologics for severe CRSwNP; however, the limited number of meta‐analyses, different inclusion criteria of the RCTs, and the scarcity of data on newer biologics constrain the strength of this evidence. Depemokimab is a promising emerging therapy with extended dosing intervals that may improve adherence, whereas omalizumab and mepolizumab have the longest‐established safety records. Notably, there are currently no recommendations supporting the use of biologics during pregnancy. A major limitation in the current literature is the lack of phase IV specifically targeting patients with comorbid CRS and asthma or the combined phenotype of N‐ERD, CRS, and asthma. Furthermore, there are very few head‐to‐head comparisons between biologics. To date, only one clinical trial in patients with severe CRSwNP and asthma has demonstrated the superiority of dupilumab over omalizumab. Omalizumab remains effective in patients with comorbid allergic asthma and may provide additional benefit when combined with AIT; however, the role of AIT in comorbid asthma and CRS remains poorly defined, despite its proven efficacy in allergic rhinitis with/without asthma. Meta‐analyses do not support the efficacy of long‐term macrolide therapy in CRS or asthma, and evidence in comorbid disease is lacking. ATAD represents an additional disease‐modifying strategy for N‐ERD; however, adherence and tolerability remain major challenges. Clinical trials assessing the impact of ATAD on CRSwNP have produced inconsistent results, even when combined with ESS, thereby limiting its broader applicability. ATAD might have some benefit in younger patients with well‐controlled asthma. Given the high rate of adverse effects associated with ATAD, there is a strong need for cost‐effectiveness and safety comparisons between ATAD (with or without ESS) and biologic therapies. Despite substantial therapeutic advances, treatment responses continue to vary according to individual phenotypes and endotypes, reinforcing the need for personalized management strategies. Significant gaps persist, including the absence of validated biomarkers to predict treatment response, safety, and optimal sequencing, as well as the lack of head‐to‐head trials comparing biologics, ATAD, and surgical approaches. Future research should focus on refining treatment algorithms, identifying predictive and prognostic biomarkers, evaluating combination and sequential therapies, and generating long‐term outcome data to optimize care for patients with comorbid CRS and asthma with/without N‐ERD. documents.title: EAACI GA2LEN EDF WAO guideline for management of chronic urticaria

chunks.content: 1 Introduction, definitions and classification Chronic Urticaria is an inflammatory skin condition predominantly mediated by mast cell activation, presenting clinically with pruritic wheals and/or angioedema lasting longer than 6 weeks. The clinical spectrum of chronic urticaria includes chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), which occurs without a known eliciting factor, and chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU), in which episodes are provoked by defined and reproducible stimuli such as physical contact, heat, cold, sunlight, pressure, friction, or vibratory ( ). The global point prevalence of CSU ranges from 0.02% to 2.7%, with female predominance and frequent associations with comorbidities such as autoimmune thyroiditis, depression, and atopic diseases. NSAIDs and stress are among the most commonly reported exacerbating factors ( ). In chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), mast cell activation is primarily driven by autoimmune mechanisms, which are currently classified into two distinct endotypes: Type I (autoallergic) CSU and Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU. Type I autoimmunity involves autoreactive IgE antibodies targeting self-antigens such as thyroid peroxidase (TPO), interleukin-24 (IL-24), thyroglobulin, and tissue transglutaminase, leading to mast cell and basophil degranulation via classical IgE–FcεRI signaling pathway. In contrast, Type IIb autoimmunity is primarily mediated by IgG autoantibodies, although IgA or IgM autoantibodies may also be involved, as demonstrated by Altrichter et al., who showed that IgM and IgA in addition to IgG autoantibodies against FcεRIα are frequent and associated with disease markers of chronic spontaneous urticaria ( , ). These antibodies target either IgE or its high-affinity receptor FcεRIα, leading to allergen-independent mast cell activation. Among these, IgG–anti-FcεRI antibodies are the most commonly implicated and demonstrate strong functional capacity to induce histamine release ( , ) Recent studies also highlights the potential pathogenic role for IgA and IgM autoantibodies, as well as frequent overlap between the two endotypes, emphasizing the immunological heterogeneity of CSU. Importantly, not all patients conform neatly to these categories; some may exhibit both IgE- and IgG-mediated autoreactivity, while others may lack detectable autoimmune markers altogether. The term autoreactivity has thus been adopted as an umbrella concept encompassing both autoimmunity and autoallergy, reflecting the evolving complexity of CSU pathophysiology ( ). Histamine, the principal effector molecule released during mast cell activation, plays a central role in the pathogenesis of chronic urticaria (CU), making H1-antihistamines the cornerstone of first-line pharmacological therapy accordance with all current treatment guidelines ( , , ). Current treatment strategies adhere to the principle of “as much as necessary, as little as possible,” with dosage tailored to disease activity and control. The primary objective is to achieve complete symptom resolution and maintain sustained remission with minimal adverse effects. International and national guidelines consistently recommend initiating therapy with second-generation H1-antihistamines (sg-AHs) due to their favorable safety profile. If standard doses of second-generation antihistamines are insufficient, dose escalation up to four fold the standard dose is recommended. However, nearly half of patients (∼55%) remain refractory to antihistamine therapy, including updosing, and subsequently require second-line treatment with the anti-IgE monoclonal antibody omalizumab. However, some patients may still be symptomatic (approximately 15%–30%), and the therapeutic response to omalizumab remains suboptimal. For this subgroup, cyclosporine represents the recommended third-line option despite its potential significant adverse effects, necessitating careful risk–benefit evaluation. In patients with Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU, cyclosporine may be considered as an alternative choice to omalizumab, particularly in those with low IgE, positive ASST/BAT, or thyroid autoantibodies, provided that risks are weighed carefully and monitoring for nephrotoxicity and hypertension is ensured ( , ). The current stepwise treatment algorithm is summarized in . 2 Immunological endotypes and pathways in CSU 2.1 Type I (autoallergic) and Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU Type I autoimmune CSU, also referred to as autoallergic CSU, is characterized by autoreactive IgE antibodies targeting self-antigens such as thyroid peroxidase (TPO), interleukin-24 (IL-24), tissue factor, thyroglobulin, double-stranded DNA, and eosinophil peroxidase ( ). Initial evidence for this autoallergic mechanism emerged in the late 1990s with the detection of IgE-anti-TPO in CSU patients. Subsequent studies confirmed the presence of IgE autoantibodies in 10%–50% of cases, depending on the target antigen and assay used ( , ). Patients with this endotype typically exhibit high total IgE levels, allergic comorbidities, and a rapid clinical response to omalizumab, as demonstrated in the X-QUISITE trial ( , ). Despite growing evidence, the clinical detection of IgE autoantibodies remains limited due to the absence of standardized and commercially available assays. In specialized research centers, in-house ELISAs are used for detecting IgE-anti-TPO or IgE-anti-IL-24, but broader accessibility and validation are still required to integrate these methods into clinical practice ( ). Evidence for IgE–anti–IL-24 as an autoallergen derives primarily from limited mechanistic work and has not yet been independently replicated; we therefore grade this as low-certainty evidence (Oxford Level 4/GRADE low) and present it accordingly in . Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU is mediated by mast cell–activating autoantibodies, primarily of the IgG

growing evidence, the clinical detection of IgE autoantibodies remains limited due to the absence of standardized and commercially available assays. In specialized research centers, in-house ELISAs are used for detecting IgE-anti-TPO or IgE-anti-IL-24, but broader accessibility and validation are still required to integrate these methods into clinical practice ( ). Evidence for IgE–anti–IL-24 as an autoallergen derives primarily from limited mechanistic work and has not yet been independently replicated; we therefore grade this as low-certainty evidence (Oxford Level 4/GRADE low) and present it accordingly in . Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU is mediated by mast cell–activating autoantibodies, primarily of the IgG isotype. These antibodies target either the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) or IgE itself, leading to mast cell degranulation and histamine release. In a subset of patients, IgG autoantibodies may also bind directly to IgE; however, these are less consistently associated with disease activity and can be detected in healthy individuals. More recently, IgA and IgM autoantibodies against FcεRI have been identified and may contribute to disease pathogenesis, particularly in patients with concurrent basopenia or eosinopenia. Both abnormalities occur in approximately 10% of CSU patients and may reflect immune cell migration to lesional skin or destruction mediated by autoantibodies. The recruited basophils and eosinophils further amplify local inflammation by releasing histamine and cytokines ( , ). Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU is generally defined by a combination of three diagnostic markers: Positive autologous serum skin test (ASST) Presence of functional IgG autoantibodies (e.g., IgG-anti-FcεRI/IgG-anti-IgE) Positive basophil activation test (BAT) or basophil histamine release assay (BHRA) ( , ). Although less prevalent diagnosed in <10% of CSU patients when strict criteria are used type IIb (autoimmune) CSU is associated with a more severe disease course, poor response to both antihistamines and omalizumab, concomitant autoimmune diseases (especially autoimmune thyroiditis and vitiligo), and low total IgE levels. Conversely, patients with this endotype tend to respond better to cyclosporine, likely due to its broad immunosuppressive action on T cells, B cells, basophils and mast cells ( ). Several emerging biomarkers have been linked to type IIb (autoimmune) CSU, including eosinopenia, basopenia, angioedema, nocturnal symptoms, and low serum IgA. The combination of IgG-anti-TPO positivity and low total IgE serves as a strong surrogate marker for this endotype, correlating well with positive BAT results and clinical refractoriness to omalizumab ( ). Key supporting evidence for these associations is summarized in . Functional assays such as BAT and BHRA remain technically demanding and are not widely available, underscoring the need for standardized and accessible testing methods to facilitate biomarker-based patient stratification. 2.2 Overlap endotypes and concept of autoreactivity Type I and Type IIb endotypes may coexist in individual CSU patients, reflecting overlapping immunopathogenic mechanisms that contribute to clinical heterogeneity and justify comprehensive serological profiling ( , ). This coexistence challenges the traditional binary view of endotypes as strictly autoallergic or autoimmune. Evidence suggests that many patients display concurrent IgE- and IgG-mediated autoreactivity to shared autoantigens such as TPO and FcεRI, supporting the concept of an immunological continuum rather than distinct subtypes ( ). This immunological heterogeneity is further supported by data-driven clinical phenotyping. In a recent machine learning–based study, Türk et al. identified four distinct clinical clusters among 431 patients with chronic urticaria. One of these, termed the “autoimmune cluster” exhibited hallmark features of type IIb (autoimmune) CSU, including high ANA (52.3%) and IgG–anti-TPO (39.8%) positivity, female predominance (92%), and frequent angioedema (77%). Another cluster resembled the autoallergic endotype with high total IgE and atopic comorbidities. These computationally derived phenotypes closely aligned with pathophysiologically defined endotypes, reinforcing the concept that CSU represents a clinical–immunological continuum rather than rigid subtypes ( ). Clinically, the overlap endotype is associated with more severe disease and delayed response to omalizumab. Patients exhibiting both IgE- and IgG-mediated autoreactivity, particularly against tissue factor or FcεRI, tend to show slower treatment responses ( ). Notably, some patients with low total IgE which typically a feature of Type IIb (autoimmune) CSU is still autoreactive IgE such as anti-FcεRI IgE or anti-TF IgE, indicating that total IgE alone may not fully reflect underlying immunologic activity ( ). These observations further support the concept that CSU exists along a continuum of immunopathology. Within this framework, autoreactivity serves as a unifying concept encompassing both IgE- and IgG-mediated immune recognition of self-antigens, which ultimately converge on mast-cell and basophil activation. This model provides a more integrated basis for biomarker-driven classification and individualized therapy in CSU ( ). Emerging data suggest that eosinophils may play a more integral role in the pathophysiology of CSU than previously assumed. Although traditionally overshadowed by mast cells and basophils, eosinophils are frequently found in lesional skin biopsies of CSU patients, especially in those with more severe or treatment-resistant disease. Recent evidence positions eosinophils as active contributors in CSU pathophysiology. The bidirectional interaction between eosinophils and mast cells is depicted in . Their presence in both lesional and non-lesional skin, especially in autoimmune or severe phenotypes, suggests a tissue-selective recruitment driven by IL-5 and eotaxins. This shift reframes eosinophils from bystanders to central effectors of inflammation ( ). The key immunopathogenic mechanisms and molecular targets involved in CSU are summarized in . Complementing these findings, Kolkhir et al. demonstrated that eosinopenia in patients with CSU is associated with type IIb autoimmunity and the presence of immunological markers such as positive ASST, ANA, and anti-TPO IgG antibodies. Moreover, eosinopenia was more frequently observed in patients with high disease activity and was suggested as a surrogate marker of both systemic immune dysregulation and therapeutic refractoriness ( ). In light of this, eosinophils emerge as dynamic participants in the inflammatory cascade, rather than inert background cells. Building upon this immunological framework, Hide and Kaplan have elucidated a link between eosinophils and activation of the extrinsic coagulation cascade in CSU. Specifically, eosinophils within urticarial lesions have been shown to express tissue factor (TF), thereby initiating thrombin generation and subsequent cleavage of complement component C5. This cascade results in the local production of C5a, a potent anaphylatoxin that activates mast cells and basophils via C5aR engagement, amplifying the inflammatory response. A schematic representation of this coagulation–complement interaction is provided in . In CSU patients, thrombin and plasmin which generated via activation of the extrinsic coagulation pathway can trigger mast cell and basophil degranulation through production of complement components C5a and C3a. These anaphylatoxins act via C5aR and C3aR on effector cells. Notably, higher levels of C5a have been consistently reported in CSU patients compared to healthy controls, pointing out the relevance of coagulation-complement crosstalk in disease amplification ( , ). Such eosinophil-driven coagulation-complement interactions not only contribute to vascular leakage and wheal formation but also help to explain systemic features and exacerbations in severe or type IIb (autoimmune) CSU phenotypes ( ). These insights also support the notion that eosinophils are not immunological epiphenomena but critical effector cells within the broader pathophysiological network of CSU. Basophils are also increasingly recognized as relevant effector cells in the immunopathogenesis of chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), complementing the well-established role of mast cells. According to Ferrer and other authors, peripheral blood basophil counts may be decreased in a subset of CSU patients, a phenomenon referred to as basopenia, which appears to be associated with heightened disease activity. Notably, this reduction has been reported to normalize during effective treatment or clinical remission. Beyond numerical alterations, functional abnormalities in basophils have also been described ( – ). CSU basophils often display a hyporesponsive phenotype to FcεRI-mediated activation, likely due to in vivo desensitization. This is accompanied by variable expression of surface activation markers such as CD63 and CD203c, although findings have been inconsistent across studies. Despite impaired anti-IgE responsiveness, these cells remain reactive to non-IgE stimuli such as C5a and fMLP, indicating a shift in activation dynamics that may contribute to therapeutic refractoriness ( ). Basophil-mediated immunopathogenic pathways are summarized in . Interestingly, even basophils that exhibit low or absent histamine release in response to FcεRI cross-linking may retain functional competence via alternative pathways.
